page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The law
lines: Law of multiple proportions (Dalton): when two
elements combine to form more than one compound,
the masses of one element that combine with a
fixed mass of the other element are in a simple
steps.why: Atoms combine in whole numbers, so if the same pair of elements forms two compounds, the second element's masses against a fixed first mass must relate as small whole numbers.
common_mistakes: Confusing this with the law of definite proportions, which is about ONE compound.
Leaving out 'fixed mass of the other element' — without it the ratio has no meaning.
steps.memory_tip: Definite: one compound, one ratio. Multiple: two compounds, whole-number ratio between them.
steps.margin_note: The phrase fixed mass of the other element must appear.

steps.label: The example

lines.text: In CO and CO₂, oxygen masses per 12 g of carbon are 16 g and 32 g — ratio 1 : 2

lines: Carbon and oxygen form two compounds;
steps.why: CO and CO₂ show the law with the smallest numbers: fixing carbon at 12 g, the combining oxygen doubles from 16 g to 32 g.
common_mistakes: Quoting the two compounds without the fixed 12 g of carbon and the two oxygen masses.
steps.memory_tip: CO to CO₂: one more oxygen atom, so exactly double the oxygen mass.
steps.margin_note: H₂O and H₂O₂ (8 g and 16 g of O per 1 g of H) is an equally accepted example.

insider_note: The example is a full mark and it must carry numbers, not just two formulas. Fixing carbon at 12 g and showing the oxygen going from 16 g to 32 g is the evidence that mark pays for.
